source_refs.note: Topic 3.8, printed pages 84-86: stem cells by potency, their uses, and embryonic, adult and induced pluripotent stem cells with the advantages and disadvantages of iPSCs.

blocks.text: Stem cells are unique cells with the remarkable ability to develop into many different cell types in the body. When a stem cell divides, each new cell has the potential either to remain a stem cell or to become a specialised cell, such as a muscle cell, a red blood cell or a brain cell.

blocks.title: Stem cell
blocks.text: A cell that can both renew itself by division and develop into one or more specialised cell types.
Categories by the number of cell types they can make

items: Totipotent: can differentiate into all possible cell types. For example, the zygote and the cells produced by the first few divisions of the zygote.
Pluripotent: can turn into almost any cell. For example, cells from the early embryo.
Multipotent: can differentiate into a closely related family of cells. For example, haematopoietic stem cells can become red and white blood cells or platelets.
Oligopotent: can differentiate into a few different cell types. For example, adult lymphoid or myeloid stem cells.
Unipotent: can only produce cells of one kind, their own type. They are still stem cells because they can renew themselves. For example, adult muscle stem cells.

Regenerative medicine: stem cells have the potential to repair or replace damaged tissues and organs, so they are used for treating conditions such as spinal cord injuries, type 1 diabetes, Parkinson's disease and heart disease.

Drug testing and development: by differentiating stem cells into specific cell types, researchers create models of human diseases, allowing more accurate testing of drug effects and reducing reliance on animal models.

Personalised medicine: stem cells can be derived from a patient's own cells, reducing the risk of immune rejection when used in treatments. This personalised approach can lead to more effective and safer therapies.

blocks.text: ESCs are derived from the inner cell mass of blastocysts (early-stage embryos). They are pluripotent, so they can differentiate into nearly all cell types in the body. Their high differentiation potential makes them extremely versatile for research and therapy. Ethical concerns about using ESCs include the use of human embryos, the risk of teratoma formation and potential immune rejection.

These stem cells are found in various tissues throughout the body, such as bone marrow, fat and blood. They are multipotent: they differentiate into a limited range of cell types related to their tissue of origin. Using them involves less ethical controversy and a lower risk of immune rejection when they are derived from the patient's own tissues. However, they have limited differentiation potential and are harder to isolate and culture.
iPSCs are generated in the laboratory by reprogramming adult somatic cells to a pluripotent state using specific transcription factors. They are pluripotent, similar to embryonic stem cells.

items: Advantages of iPSCs: they do not carry the ethical controversies linked to embryonic stem cells, since they do not require the destruction of embryos. They can be generated from a patient's own cells, minimising the risk of immune rejection. They offer potential for regenerating damaged tissues and organs, such as new heart cells for patients with heart disease or new neurons for patients with neurodegenerative conditions.

Disadvantages of iPSCs: the reprogramming process can introduce genetic changes that may affect the iPSCs. They could form tumours (teratomas) when transplanted into patients. Directing iPSCs to differentiate into specific, fully functional cell types remains a complex task, and it is still difficult to ensure that these cells function properly.

Right, three sources: a blastocyst for embryonic stem cells, a bone for adult stem cells, and an adult cell reprogrammed with transcription factors into an induced pluripotent stem cell, with their advantages and disadvantages.
blocks.caption: Stem cells by potency and by source (original diagram after Figure 3.39).
blocks.long_description: By potency: totipotent cells (zygote and its first divisions) make all cell types; pluripotent cells (early embryo) almost any; multipotent cells (haematopoietic stem cells) a related family; oligopotent cells (lymphoid, myeloid) a few; unipotent cells (muscle stem cells) one type. By source: embryonic stem cells from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst are pluripotent but raise ethical concerns and risks of teratoma and rejection; adult stem cells from bone marrow, fat and blood are multipotent, less controversial and low-rejection if the patient's own, but limited and hard to culture; induced pluripotent stem cells are adult somatic cells reprogrammed with transcription factors, avoiding embryo destruction and rejection but risking genetic changes and teratomas and being hard to direct.

blocks.prompt: Classify: (a) a zygote, (b) a haematopoietic stem cell, (c) an adult muscle stem cell, (d) a cell from an early embryo. Then say which source of stem cells avoids both embryo destruction and immune rejection, and name one risk of using it.
blocks.explanation: (a) Totipotent. (b) Multipotent. (c) Unipotent. (d) Pluripotent. Induced pluripotent stem cells avoid both, because they are made from the patient's own adult cells; risks include genetic changes from reprogramming and teratoma formation.

items: A stem cell renews itself and can specialise. By potency: totipotent (zygote), pluripotent (early embryo), multipotent (blood stem cells), oligopotent (lymphoid, myeloid), unipotent (muscle stem cells).
Uses: regenerative medicine, drug testing on disease models, personalised medicine from the patient's own cells.

By origin: embryonic (pluripotent; ethical concerns, teratoma, rejection), adult (multipotent; fewer ethical issues, low rejection, but limited and hard to culture), induced pluripotent (reprogrammed adult cells; no embryos, low rejection, but genetic changes, teratomas and hard to direct).
